questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Enzyme data: rate proxy against temperature
questions.scenario: A fictional teacher dataset reports times to an indicator endpoint for the same substrate amount: 240, 140, 80, 50, 100 and 240 s at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C respectively. The graph plots 1/t, a relative proxy rather than an independently calibrated reaction rate.
tasks: (a) State the temperature with the highest model rate proxy.
(b) Calculate 1/t at 20 °C (3 significant figures).
(c) Describe the trend and give two limitations or controls.
marks: The peak of this particular model dataset is at 40 °C.
The rate proxy rises up to 40 °C.
It declines in the model data beyond 40 °C.
1/t is a comparative endpoint proxy, not an absolute initial rate; a single trial does not prove a universal temperature optimum.
Temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme preparation should be controlled or independently checked when interpreting comparisons.
questions.worked_explanation: At 40 °C, t=50 s so 1/t=0.0200 s⁻¹. At 60 °C, t=240 s so 1/t≈0.00417 s⁻¹; these are relative measures for equal endpoint criteria.
questions.common_error: Interpreting a 1/t peak as the exact optimum for every amylase sample or as direct evidence for one mechanism.
questions.transfer_question: If the endpoint time were 125 s, calculate the rate proxy.
questions.model_assumption: Assume identical endpoint criterion and substrate quantity; all numbers are hypothetical.

questions.title: Photosynthesis evidence and confounding variables

plot.y_label: Collected gas volume per minute (mm³ min⁻¹)

questions.scenario: A fictional teacher dataset reports a gas-collection proxy at different lamp distances for an aquatic-plant model. The identity of gas is assumed by the teaching model; temperature and dissolved inorganic carbon were not independently measured.
tasks: (a) State the direction of association between distance and collected gas.
(b) Determine the decrease from 10 to 50 cm and its percentage of the 10 cm value.
(c) Identify two reasons not to equate this graph with an exact light-response law.
marks: Collected gas per minute decreases as lamp distance increases in this dataset.
Gas collection is a proxy, not necessarily a direct measure of carbon fixation.
Lamp geometry, absorption, reflection and scattering prevent inference of a precise inverse-square relationship from these measurements alone.
Temperature or dissolved CO₂ can also change the result unless accounted for.

questions.common_error: Drawing a precise inverse-square law from lamp distance alone or assuming all collected gas is confirmed oxygen.

questions.title: Initial-rate graph: what order can actually be inferred?

plot.x_label: Model concentration of reactant A (mol dm⁻³)

questions.scenario: A classroom model varies A while another reactant B, temperature and total conditions are fixed. The plotted initial rates are labelled in arbitrary units, so this exercise concerns proportionality and conditional reaction order.

(b) Determine the order in A under the stated controlled conditions.
(c) State what cannot be inferred about B or the rate constant.
marks: When A doubles, observed initial rate rises from 0.5 to 1.0 units.
Under fixed B and temperature, doubling A doubles the rate, consistent with first order in A.

questions.scenario: A biology teacher provides three written descriptions of fictional animal-tissue micrographs.
questions.question: Identify A, B and C and give two specific discriminating observations.
marks: Intercalated discs and branching help distinguish cardiac from skeletal muscle.
The absence of striations and spindle shape help distinguish smooth muscle.
questions.error: Assuming that all striated tissues are skeletal muscle.
questions.transfer: Why would “striated” alone be an insufficient identification of skeletal muscle?
questions.transfer_answer: Cardiac muscle also displays striations; check branching, nuclei and intercalated discs.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Exercise responses: paired comparisons
questions.scenario: Two fictional students supplied pulse-rate observations in a teacher-run classroom illustration. The activities and timing were described as comparable.
questions.question: Calculate the mean pulse rise from rest to immediately afterward, then the mean fall during recovery. Give one reason not to generalise.
marks: 3-min mean = 86 bpm; fall from immediately after = 114 − 86 = 28 bpm.
Only two subjects and incomplete control of fitness/intensity limit generalisation.
questions.error: Mixing heart rate in beats per minute with respiratory rate in breaths per minute.
questions.transfer: If average heart rate is 80 bpm at rest and 104 bpm later, what is the increase?

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Interpreting inhibitory-zone evidence
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies an already-completed, fictional illustration of comparative inhibitory zones. No students are asked to culture organisms or handle disinfectants.
questions.question: State the limited observation, one conditional comparison and two reasons it does not rank overall real-world antimicrobial effectiveness.
marks: A shows a larger clear-zone diameter than B within this single dataset.
C and the negative control show no measured clear zone under the model conditions.
A larger zone is compatible with greater inhibition under these particular assay conditions.
Zone size also depends on how test substances diffuse through the medium.
The dataset alone cannot establish clinical effectiveness, safety, sterility or general superiority.
questions.error: Treating one inhibition-zone image as proof that an agent sterilises surfaces or is safe for personal use.
questions.transfer: If a substance has a small clear zone because it diffuses slowly, what can you conclude about its intrinsic potency?
questions.transfer_answer: Not enough; diffusion and potency can affect zones differently. A separate controlled comparison is required.
questions.provenance: Artificial teaching worksheet; no experimental instruction.
questions.alignment_note: The earlier inhibition-zone exercise is associated microbiology practice, not the colony-count method in NIE Biology Practical38. PM5-B38 now provides method-aligned colony-count practice.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Burette reading and stated uncertainty
questions.scenario: A fictional teacher dataset states the uncertainty of each burette reading explicitly. Use the worst-case absolute-uncertainty convention.
questions.question: Determine the delivered volume and its absolute and approximate relative uncertainty.
marks: The delivered volume is found from the difference of two readings.
Final presentation: (24.60 ± 0.10) cm³ under the stated convention.
questions.error: Assigning only one single-reading uncertainty to a difference of two readings.
questions.transfer: Find the delivered volume if the initial reading is 1.20 cm³ and final reading is 23.75 cm³.
questions.provenance: Invented instrument readings and explicitly stated uncertainties.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Gas quantity from a teacher-supplied dataset
questions.scenario: For this theoretical question, assume the measured gas behaves ideally. No actual gas collection is required.
questions.question: Determine n using pV = nRT and explain why the volume must be converted before substitution in SI units.
marks: Using dm³ with Pa and SI R without consistent conversion causes a factor-of-1000 error.
questions.error: Using temperature in degrees Celsius in an ideal-gas equation that requires absolute temperature.
questions.transfer: At fixed amount and pressure in the ideal model, what happens to the gas volume when absolute temperature increases from 300 K to 360 K?

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Hess cycle with a reversed step
questions.scenario: A symbolic reaction network contains hypothetical reactions with matching stoichiometric normalisation; A, B and C stand for appropriately defined chemical states.
questions.question: Calculate ΔH for A → C and C → A. Explain the sign change.
marks: By Hess's law, add the two consecutive step enthalpies.
The A → C model reaction is exothermic.
Reversing the net reaction reverses the enthalpy sign.
questions.error: Reversing a reaction arrow without also reversing ΔH.
questions.transfer: If a known reaction is +17 kJ mol⁻¹, what is the enthalpy change of the exactly reversed reaction?
questions.provenance: Symbolic model reactions, not laboratory enthalpy results.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Evidence of a changed coordination environment
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies imaginary spectroscopic summaries for a transition-metal solution. Temperature, concentration and path length are not independently controlled.
questions.question: Explain what the spectral shift suggests and give limitations on interpreting visible colour alone.
marks: The model shows a change in the reported absorption maximum from 520 to 600 nm.
Transition-metal absorption can change when the ligand/coordination environment changes.
A shift is consistent with a changed electronic-energy splitting in a complex.
Colour or one absorption maximum alone cannot uniquely determine ligand identity or coordination number.
Uncontrolled concentration, temperature or pH and overlapping species can complicate interpretation.
questions.error: Naming a particular complex or coordination number solely from an observed colour.
questions.transfer: A second sample has the same visible colour. Does that prove it contains the identical complex?
questions.transfer_answer: No. Different species and mixtures can appear similar; further independent evidence is needed.
questions.provenance: Hypothetical spectroscopy only; no chemical manipulation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Predicting salt-solution acidity conceptually
questions.scenario: Assume dilute aqueous solutions at ordinary laboratory conditions. No measured pH values are provided.
questions.question: Classify each solution as acidic, basic or approximately neutral. Explain the responsible ions.
marks: NH4Cl is expected to give an acidic solution.
NH4+ is a conjugate acid capable of acidifying water; Cl− is approximately spectator.
Na2CO3 is expected to give a basic solution.
CO3²− is a base capable of accepting a proton from water.
NaCl is approximately neutral under the model, since Na+ and Cl− do not significantly hydrolyse.
questions.error: Automatically classifying every ionic compound solution as neutral.
questions.transfer: Predict whether an NH4NO3 solution is acidic, basic or approximately neutral.
questions.transfer_answer: Acidic, primarily because of NH4+; NO3− is approximately spectator.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: An apparent partition ratio
questions.scenario: These numbers are an imaginary snapshot of two phases. Acid association and dissociation are not established by the question.
questions.question: Calculate the observed organic-to-aqueous concentration ratio. Why might it not be a fundamental distribution constant?
marks: Define the observed ratio as organic concentration divided by aqueous concentration.
It is dimensionless when concentrations have the same units.
Ethanoic acid can associate in some organic phases and dissociate in water.
Without controlling chemical species, pH and equilibrium conditions, total-concentration ratio need not be a universal constant.
questions.error: Claiming a unique thermodynamic distribution coefficient from total concentrations without stating species assumptions.
questions.transfer: A similar fictional ratio uses 0.160 mol dm⁻³ in organic and 0.080 mol dm⁻³ in water. Find the observed ratio.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Standard potential versus cell voltage
questions.scenario: A classroom reference table gives the two hypothetical standard reduction potentials, with the conventional sign and ideal standard-state assumptions.
questions.question: Identify anode and cathode and find E°cell, noting what positive voltage does not establish.
marks: Cu²+/Cu has the more positive reduction potential and is the cathode in the spontaneous galvanic direction.
Zn/Zn²+ is the oxidation half-cell (anode) in that direction.
Positive E°cell under standard-state assumptions is not a rate measurement or a guarantee about real non-standard behaviour.
questions.error: Adding two tabulated reduction potentials without considering which electrode is the anode.
questions.transfer: Using E°(Cu²+/Cu)=+0.34 V and E°(Fe²+/Fe)=−0.44 V, find the standard galvanic E°cell.
questions.provenance: Conventional reference values presented as a teaching model.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Dissolved oxygen from a stoichiometric report
questions.scenario: The teacher provides already-processed numerical results for a Winkler-method case. This is calculation only, not an instruction for handling reagents.
questions.question: Estimate the dissolved oxygen concentration in mg L⁻¹. Assume the stated stoichiometry applies and oxygen molar mass is 32.0 g mol⁻¹.
marks: Convert to 0.960 mg O2 in 0.2000 L sample.
DO = 0.960/0.2000 = 4.80 mg L⁻¹ under the idealised assumptions.
questions.error: Forgetting the 1:4 mole relationship or the final division by sample volume in litres.
questions.transfer: For a 200.0 cm³ sample with 8.00 cm³ of 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ thiosulfate, what would the same model yield?
questions.provenance: Illustrative processed titration values; no live water sample.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Correcting a signed zero error
questions.scenario: A signed zero error is explicitly provided by the teacher. The instrument has otherwise been read correctly.
questions.question: Find the corrected value and state the general sign convention.
marks: The correction relationship is true/corrected = observed − signed zero error.
Signed zero error here is +0.02 cm.
State the answer with a length unit and consistent precision.
A positive zero error must be subtracted; do not also apply a second zero correction.
questions.error: Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting it.
questions.transfer: If displayed reading is 3.12 cm and signed zero error is −0.01 cm, give corrected reading.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Moment balance about a pivot
questions.scenario: Two vertical forces act downward on opposite sides of a horizontal beam with a frictionless pivot. Neglect beam weight or treat its moment as zero. The beam is at rest.
questions.question: Determine the unknown force using moments and justify the lever-arm quantity.
marks: For equilibrium, the resultant moment about the pivot is zero.
Clockwise moment equals anticlockwise moment in magnitude.
Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action.
F = 3.0 N for this simplified model.
questions.error: Using an oblique length instead of a perpendicular distance, or adding moments with the wrong directions.
questions.transfer: If 1.5 N acts 0.20 m left and an unknown force acts 0.15 m right in equilibrium, find the unknown.
questions.provenance: Idealised force diagram as a data table.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Testing a mass-spring period relationship
questions.scenario: An ideal spring model assumes negligible spring effective mass, small oscillations and approximately Hooke-law behaviour.
questions.question: Compute T²/m for each case, infer the approximate spring constant k from T²/m = 4π²/k, and explain a limitation.
marks: Near agreement supports T² proportional to m within the supplied precision.
Effective spring mass and non-ideal oscillations limit a two-point model.
questions.error: Plotting T instead of T² without checking the expected linear form.
questions.transfer: Under the ideal relation T ∝ √m, what happens to T when m is doubled?
questions.correction_note: Corrected spring constant rounding: using the mean T²/m gives 9.95735 N m⁻¹, hence 9.96 to three significant figures. Historical attempts retain their original text.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Resonance spacing and speed of sound
questions.scenario: A fictional closed-tube model supplies first and second resonance lengths at the same frequency. Assume one open end, one closed end and the same positive end correction.
questions.question: Infer wavelength and wave speed. Explain why using the separation reduces dependence on a fixed end correction.
marks: Successive resonances differ in tube length by λ/2.
A constant end correction cancels in the difference; here e = λ/4 − 0.17 = +0.005 m.
questions.error: Interpreting the difference between successive closed-tube resonances as one full wavelength.
questions.transfer: For successive resonances 0.40 m apart at 400 Hz, infer the speed.
questions.correction_note: The earlier 0.18 m and 0.53 m first/second lengths implied a negative end correction. V5 uses 0.17 m and 0.52 m: the same spacing and speed, with a physically valid +0.005 m end correction.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Minimum deviation and prism refractive index
questions.scenario: Assume a prism in air and the standard minimum-deviation geometry for the refractive index of its material.
questions.question: Estimate n with n = sin[(A + Dmin)/2]/sin(A/2) and name the assumption essential to the formula.
marks: At minimum deviation, use n = sin[(A + Dmin)/2]/sin(A/2).
The formula assumes the minimum-deviation configuration and a surrounding medium effectively of refractive index 1.
questions.error: Substituting angles into a calculator in radians when the input is expressed in degrees.
questions.transfer: For A=60° and Dmin=30°, find n to three significant figures.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: A gas graph should use absolute temperature
questions.scenario: An imaginary fixed-mass gas dataset assumes approximately constant pressure and ideal behaviour over the limited measured range.
questions.question: Test whether V/T is approximately constant. Estimate the volume at 360 K and explain why extrapolation to 0 K is not a literal experimental prediction.
marks: The values support V ∝ T for the limited model data.
Real gases may condense or depart from the ideal model before 0 K is approached.
questions.error: Using a Celsius scale in the direct-proportionality relation V ∝ absolute temperature.
questions.transfer: At fixed pressure, what model volume corresponds to 450 K if the volume is 100 cm³ at 300 K?
questions.provenance: Synthetic gas data, not a real apparatus result.

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Potentiometer emf comparison
questions.scenario: The teacher reports ideal null-point lengths on the same uniform potentiometer wire with unchanged current and potential gradient.
questions.question: Estimate E1/E2 and explain why the common gradient cancels.
marks: At balance E = kL for the same uniform potential gradient k.
Report that Cell 1 EMF is about 0.813 times Cell 2 under the assumptions.
At ideal null, no current is drawn from the test cell, limiting loading effects.
questions.error: Using the reciprocal length ratio without checking which EMF is in the numerator.
questions.transfer: What is E1/E2 for null lengths 70.0 cm and 100.0 cm?

questions.subject: physics
questions.title: Logic gate identification from all input pairs
questions.scenario: A teacher provides the full theoretical truth table for a two-input logic device.
questions.question: Identify the gate and give its Boolean relationship. Explain why omitting one row could create ambiguity.
marks: The output is also 1 for (0,1) and (1,0).
The device is a NAND gate: Y = NOT(A AND B).
A full truth table tests all possible input pairs and distinguishes NAND from other logical functions.
questions.error: Calling the device an OR gate because the three other rows look similar; OR differs at (0,0) and (1,1).
questions.transfer: If this NAND output is inverted by a NOT gate, which logical operation results?
questions.transfer_answer: AND, because NOT(NOT(A AND B)) = A AND B.
questions.provenance: Theoretical truth table; no electricity experiment needed.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Respiratory quotient: a ratio is not an identification
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A fictional teacher dataset shows that germinating seeds used 45.0 cm3 of oxygen while producing 36.0 cm3 of carbon dioxide during the same observation interval. Assume both readings were corrected to comparable temperature and pressure.
tasks: Calculate the respiratory quotient, with its unit status.
Explain what this value suggests about the respiratory substrate.
Identify two reasons why the measurement does not uniquely identify the substrate.
marks: RQ = CO₂ volume / O₂ volume over the same interval.
RQ is dimensionless for comparable gas volumes.
RQ 0.800 is compatible with protein or mixed-substrate oxidation; it is not specific evidence of fat alone.
It does not prove that only one substrate was respired.
Mixed substrates can produce intermediate quotients.
Gas dissolution and measurement limitations can bias the sampled RQ.
Compare gas volumes at equivalent temperature and pressure.
questions.common_error: Inferring a unique organic substrate solely from RQ.
questions.transfer_question: For another hypothetical data pair, CO2=30.0 cm3 and O2=40.0 cm3. Find RQ and state what cannot be concluded.
questions.transfer_answer: 0.750; it does not uniquely identify the substrate.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Potometer data: uptake is not identical to transpiration
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies hypothetical observations from a very narrow capillary: inner radius 0.250 mm, bubble displacement 80.0 mm in 5.00 min. Assume a circular cross-section and no change in tube radius.
tasks: Calculate the volume of water movement and rate in mm3 min-1.
Express the rate in microlitres per minute.
Explain why this need not equal actual transpiration at that instant.
marks: Volume = area x distance = 0.19635 x 80.0 = 15.7 mm3.
1 mm3 = 1 microlitre, so rate = 3.14 microlitres min-1.
The measured variable is capillary water uptake (a proxy).
Some water can be used or stored in tissues.
Environmental conditions can change water loss during measurement.
Measurement uncertainty in radius is magnified by the squared-radius term.
questions.common_error: Treating the water-uptake proxy as a direct, universally equal measurement of transpiration.
questions.transfer_question: If the measured inner radius is doubled while bubble speed is unchanged, by what factor does inferred flow change?
questions.transfer_answer: Factor of four: volume rate is proportional to cross-sectional area, and area is proportional to r2.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Electron-image scale: recalibrate after resizing
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: On an illustrative printed micrograph, a scale bar representing 40.0 micrometres measures 20.0 mm on the page. An organelle on that same image spans 7.50 mm. The worksheet was not calibrated to a real specimen.
tasks: Calculate the enlargement of this particular printed image.
Estimate the represented organelle length.
State why the displayed page enlargement is not an intrinsic property of the original specimen.
marks: The scale ratio is 40.0 micrometres / 20.0 mm = 2.00 micrometres per mm.
Units of bar and image length must be converted before division.
Resizing a document changes the printed enlargement.
Resizing both scale bar and image together preserves the inferred specimen size.
A calibration bar is more reliable than claiming a fixed enlargement after a rescaled export.

questions.transfer_question: If the entire image is enlarged to twice its printed dimensions, what is the new printed enlargement and the inferred organelle length?
questions.transfer_answer: 1,000 times and still 15.0 micrometres, provided the scale bar enlarges with the image.

questions.subject: biology
questions.title: Plasmolysis threshold: interpolation is an estimate
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: A fictional slide-count dataset reports 20% of cells classified as plasmolysed at 0.20 mol dm-3 and 55% at 0.30 mol dm-3. No observations were made between these two concentrations.
tasks: Find the concentration estimated to give 50% plasmolysis by linear interpolation.
Explain why the answer is not an exact experimental concentration.
State what extra information is needed to infer solute potential.
marks: Needed rise from 20% to 50% is 30 percentage points.
The estimate assumes approximately linear behaviour in this interval.
Cell classification and sampling variation require uncertainty or more points.
Solute potential needs temperature, effective solute-particle concentration and a justified physicochemical model; concentration alone is not a reported potential.
questions.common_error: Reporting an interpolated 50% level as though it was directly measured or universally fixed.
questions.transfer_question: At 0.20 mol dm-3 35% are plasmolysed, at 0.30 mol dm-3 60%. Estimate the 50% threshold.
questions.transfer_answer: 0.20 + (15/25) x 0.10 = 0.260 mol dm-3 under linear interpolation.
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.title: Calorimetry: heat gained versus reaction enthalpy
questions.dataset_status: FICTIONAL TEACHER-WRITTEN EXAMPLE - not observed in a laboratory
questions.scenario: An already-completed fictional teacher dataset reports a 50.0 g solution warming from 22.5 C to 28.0 C. Use c=4.18 J g-1 K-1 and 0.0250 mol of reaction as defined by its stoichiometric extent. Suppose a hypothetical calorimeter heat capacity is 45.0 J K-1.
tasks: Calculate the heat gained by the solution.
Calculate the inferred molar reaction enthalpy first neglecting, then including, the calorimeter heat capacity.
Explain one remaining cause of underestimating the exothermic magnitude.
marks: Solution heat = mc DeltaT = 50.0 x 4.18 x 5.5 = 1.15 kJ.
Neglecting calorimeter, reaction DeltaH = -1.1495/0.0250 = -46.0 kJ mol-1.
Including the calorimeter, ΔH = −1397 J / 0.0250 mol = −55880 J mol⁻¹ = −55.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
The minus sign indicates exothermic reaction under the stated model.
Energy lost to surroundings before observation of the peak is not included and can further underestimate the magnitude.
questions.common_error: Equating heat gained by solution alone to total reaction heat without stating the calorimeter/loss assumptions.
questions.transfer_question: If the calorimeter heat capacity were 0, what would be the inferred DeltaH for this data?
questions.evidence_limit: Numerical work verified by automated checks where applicable; contextual interpretation is an independent study explanation.

questions.practical_title: Detecting the main classes of biological food molecules
questions.title: Food-test records: a negative result is not an absence
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies completed, fictional test records for four unlabelled food samples. No student handling of reagents is involved.
questions.question: Identify the food class indicated for P, Q, R and S, and explain why the direct Benedict's result for Q does not show that sugar is absent.
marks: P contains a reducing sugar: Benedict's reagent gives a brick-red (orange-red) precipitate on heating.
Q is consistent with a non-reducing sugar: it is negative directly but positive after hydrolysis releases reducing sugars.
R contains starch: iodine solution turns blue-black.
S contains protein: the biuret test gives a violet / purple colour (peptide bonds in alkaline copper(II) solution).

A direct negative Benedict's result means no reducing sugar was detected under those test conditions; it does not exclude all sugars. Q becoming positive after hydrolysis and neutralisation supports a non-reducing sugar. These tests are qualitative, with detection limits.
questions.mistake: Reporting "no sugar" from a negative direct Benedict's test without the hydrolysis comparison.
questions.tq: A sample dissolved in ethanol gives a white cloudy emulsion when the solution is poured into water. Which food class is indicated?
questions.ta: Lipid (the ethanol emulsion test): the cloudy white emulsion is dispersed lipid droplets.

B is the most likely cyanobacterium: filamentous, blue-green pigmentation throughout the cell, and no chloroplasts.
C is eukaryotic: a distinct nucleus and a chloroplast are visible, and its cells are ten times wider than A (10.0 ÷ 1.0).
Cyanobacteria photosynthesise but are prokaryotes, so their pigments are in the cytoplasm / thylakoids, not in chloroplasts, and they have no membrane-bound nucleus.

These routine light-microscope descriptions do not reliably resolve a bacterial nucleoid or establish nuclear organisation from absence alone; combine size, pigmentation and arrangement. A nucleoid is not a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.scenario: A fictional printed TEM image of a rod-shaped bacterium has a scale bar labelled 0.50 µm that measures 15.0 mm on the page. On the same page the cell is 48.0 mm long and 20.0 mm wide, and its flagellum measures 90.0 mm.

questions.title: Plant cell types: wall, living status and function
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional notes on five plant cell types seen in prepared sections.
questions.question: Identify A to E, and explain how wall thickness and living status are related to the function of each.
marks: A is parenchyma: thin-walled living cells that store material and carry out metabolism.

B is collenchyma: living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls provide flexible support. C is a sclerenchyma fibre: typically dead at maturity, with thick lignified secondary walls providing rigid support.
D is a xylem vessel element: lignified, dead and hollow, forming a tube for water transport.
E is a phloem sieve-tube element: living, with sieve plates and a companion cell, transporting sugars.

questions.title: Dicot wood: ring widths and the limits of ring counting
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies a fictional cross-section of a dicot tree stem with five rings, assumed annual. Widths are listed from the pith outward, so ring 1 is the innermost.
questions.question: Calculate the mean ring width, identify the widest and narrowest rings, state where the vascular cambium adds new tissue, and explain why counting rings may not give age in some tropical trees.
marks: Total radial increment represented by the five rings = 2.0 + 3.0 + 2.5 + 1.0 + 1.5 = 10.0 mm; mean ring width = 10.0/5 = 2.00 mm per ring.
Ring 4 is narrowest (1.0 mm) and ring 2 widest (3.0 mm, 1.5 times the mean); width shows growth rate only, not its cause (rainfall, shade or damage).
The vascular cambium makes secondary xylem on its inner side and secondary phloem on its outer side, so wood accumulates inward and ring 1 is the oldest.
Secondary xylem is a complex tissue. Its mature vessel elements/tracheids are dead and lignified for water transport/support, while xylem parenchyma can remain alive.
In weakly seasonal tropical climates the cambium may be active all year or in several bursts, giving indistinct or false rings, so counts need independent evidence.
questions.mistake: Treating the outermost ring as the oldest.
questions.tq: A wood radius of 12.0 mm contains six equal rings. What is each ring width?

questions.title: Circulation: cardiac output and vessel structure
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional values for one person and two vessel descriptions. Vessel A has a thick, elastic, muscular wall, a narrow lumen and a pulse. Vessel B has a thin wall, a wide lumen and valves.
questions.question: Calculate cardiac output at rest and during exercise in dm³ min⁻¹, find the factor of increase, and identify vessels A and B with one structural reason each.
marks: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
At rest: 72 × 70 = 5040 cm³ min⁻¹ = 5.04 dm³ min⁻¹.
During exercise: 140 × 100 = 14 000 cm³ min⁻¹ = 14.0 dm³ min⁻¹, a factor of 14.0 ÷ 5.04 = 2.78.
Both changes contribute: heart rate rises by a factor of 1.94 and stroke volume by 1.43.
A is an artery (thick elastic muscular wall withstands pulsing high pressure) and B is a vein (thin wall, valves prevent backflow at low pressure).

questions.practical_title: Organization of the human nervous system
questions.title: Nervous system: reflex arc timing
questions.scenario: A fictional monosynaptic spinal-reflex model has a sensory neuron 0.80 m long and a motor neuron 0.80 m long; both conduct at 80 m s⁻¹. One direct sensory-to-motor spinal synapse adds 1.0 ms. Receptor activation, neuromuscular transmission and muscle response delays are excluded. A separately supplied voluntary-response time is 200 ms. This is an associated theoretical timing exercise, not the gross-anatomy method specified in NIE Practical 28.
questions.question: Put the reflex-arc components in order, calculate the total reflex time, compare it with the voluntary response, and state one limitation.
marks: For this specified monosynaptic model: receptor → sensory neuron → one direct sensory-to-motor synapse in spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle effector; no spinal interneuron is included.
Total reflex time = 20 ms + 1.0 ms synaptic delay = 21 ms.
200/21 = 9.52, approximately 9.5 times as long. Additional processing can contribute to a voluntary-response delay, but these two timing values do not independently identify its precise mechanisms.
Limitation: conduction velocity depends on myelination and fibre diameter, and receptor and muscle delays were ignored.

questions.title: Sensory receptors: reading two-point threshold data
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional class-mean values for the smallest separation of two touch points that is felt as two points.
questions.question: State which region has the finest discrimination, calculate how many times coarser the back is than the fingertip, explain the pattern, and state one limitation.
marks: A smaller threshold means finer discrimination, so the fingertip (2 mm) discriminates best.
Back ÷ fingertip = 45 ÷ 2 = 22.5, so the back is 22.5 times coarser.
Regions with more touch receptors per unit area, and larger representation in the sensory cortex, can resolve closer points.
Touch receptors are mechanoreceptors: deformation produces a generator potential which can trigger action potentials in the sensory neuron.
Limitation: the reports are subjective and class means hide individual variation; pressure and attention also affect results.
questions.mistake: Concluding that a larger number means better sensitivity.

questions.title: Eye and ear: pupil area and the route of sound
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional values: the pupil diameter is 2.0 mm in bright light and 6.0 mm in dim light.
questions.question: Calculate the pupil area in each light level and the ratio, name the iris muscles responsible for the change, and list the route of sound from the pinna to the nerve signal.
marks: Area = π(d ÷ 2)²: bright light π(1.0)² = 3.14 mm², dim light π(3.0)² = 28.3 mm².

Pupil-area ratio = (6.0/2.0)² = 9.0. At equal incident irradiance this aperture-area increase would admit about nine times the light; actual bright-versus-dim light flux cannot be calculated from pupil diameters alone.
In bright light the circular iris muscles contract (smaller pupil); in dim light the radial muscles contract (larger pupil); the two sets act antagonistically.
Sound route: pinna, ear canal, tympanic membrane, ear ossicles, oval window, fluid in the cochlea, hair cells, auditory nerve.
Limitation: pupil size is only one of several adjustments to light level; the retina also adapts, so the area ratio is not the whole change in sensitivity.
questions.mistake: Comparing diameters (a factor of 3) and forgetting that area depends on diameter squared.
questions.tq: The pupil diameter changes from 3.0 mm to 6.0 mm. By what factor does its area change?

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional diagram notes. P: coiled tubules inside the testis in which sperm form. Q: a tightly coiled tube on the surface of the testis. questions.question: Name P, Q, R and S with their functions, and use the temperature values to explain the position of the testes.
marks: P is the seminiferous tubules: sperm are produced here.
Q is the epididymis: sperm mature and are stored.
R is the vas deferens: muscular contractions carry sperm toward the urethra.
S is the seminal vesicle: its fluid contains fructose that supplies energy to sperm.
The scrotum is 37.0 − 34.5 = 2.5 °C cooler than the core; sperm production is temperature sensitive, so this cooler site supports it.

questions.title: Female reproductive system: reading a hormone timeline
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional timeline notes for a model 28-day menstrual cycle.
questions.question: State when ovulation is expected and explain why, name the structure that secretes progesterone after ovulation, explain what low progesterone on day 28 allows, and state a limitation of the day numbers.
marks: Ovulation is expected shortly after the LH surge on day 14.
Rising oestrogen from the developing follicle (peak on day 13) triggers the LH surge through positive feedback.
The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle, secretes progesterone, which maintains the thickened endometrium.
If there is no pregnancy the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium breaks down (menstruation).
Limitation: this is a model 28-day cycle; cycle length varies between people and cycles, so these day numbers cannot predict ovulation for an individual.
questions.mistake: Placing ovulation on day 1 of the cycle or confusing the follicle with the corpus luteum.

B is cervical: the transverse foramina allow the vertebral arteries to pass.

questions.title: Appendicular skeleton and movement: the forearm as a lever
questions.scenario: A fictional forearm lever model is at rest. The biceps force has a perpendicular moment arm of 0.040 m about the elbow; a 20.0 N external load has a perpendicular moment arm of 0.300 m. Neglect forearm weight. The model includes only biceps force, external load and the elbow reaction. This associated biomechanics exercise extends the handbook skeletal-model observations.
questions.question: Use moments about the elbow to find the force in the biceps, state the mechanical advantage, name the joint type with the antagonistic muscle, and state a limitation.
marks: Moments about the elbow balance: F × 0.040 = 20.0 × 0.300.
Mechanical advantage = 0.040 ÷ 0.300 = 0.133, so the muscle force is 7.5 times the load.
The elbow is a hinge joint (movement in one plane); the triceps is the antagonist that extends the forearm while the biceps flexes it.
Limitation: the forearm weight, the angle of pull and tendon elasticity were ignored, so 150 N is a model estimate.
questions.mistake: Taking moments about the load instead of the pivot, or using the longer distance in the denominator.
questions.tq: The load is moved to 0.250 m from the elbow. What is the biceps force?

questions.title: Sterilisation: survivor data and choosing methods
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional survivor counts for a resistant spore culture held at a fixed high temperature. This question analyses data; it is not a sterilisation protocol.
questions.question: Calculate the time for each tenfold reduction (D-value), the time for a 12-log reduction under the same conditions, and match culture medium, glassware, an inoculating needle and a heat-sensitive solution to suitable methods.
marks: Each 5 min gives a 100-fold (2-log) reduction, so 0.40 log per minute and D = 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5 min per tenfold reduction.
A 12-log reduction needs 12 × 2.5 = 30 min if the line stays straight.
Culture medium: steam under pressure (autoclave); glassware: dry heat in a hot-air oven; inoculating needle: flaming in a flame.
A heat-sensitive solution cannot be heated, so it is filtered through a membrane filter small enough to retain bacteria.
Limitation: real survivor curves can have shoulders and tails, so a straight-line extrapolation can understate the time needed.
questions.mistake: Reading a 2-log fall in 5 minutes as a 2-fold fall.
questions.tq: If D = 3.0 min, how long is needed for a 6-log reduction?
questions.subject: biology
questions.error: Reading a 2-log fall in 5 minutes as a 2-fold fall.
questions.transfer: If D = 3.0 min, how long is needed for a 6-log reduction?
questions.alignment_note: Theoretical D-value arithmetic correct and conditional. Low expected survivors do not guarantee sterility. A membrane suitable for bacteria need not remove every virus or dissolved toxin; wording should not make an unrestricted guarantee. No actual temperature supplied; not an operating protocol.

questions.title: Culture medium and plate counts: working out viable counts
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results from plating 0.100 cm³ portions of tenfold dilutions of a yoghurt suspension on nutrient medium, after incubation.
questions.question: Select the plate within the stated illustrative 30–300-colony counting range. Calculate CFU per cm³ of the original suspension, compare the low-count plate estimate, and state two limitations. This is associated quantitative culture-data enrichment, not the handbook streak-plate morphology method.
marks: Use a plate with a countable number of colonies (usually 30 to 300): the 10⁻³ plate with 45.
The 10⁻⁴ plate gives 5 ÷ (0.100 × 10⁻⁴) = 5.0 × 10⁵, consistent, but five colonies is too few to be statistically reliable.
A colony may arise from a cell clump, so CFU need not equal individual-cell number; only organisms forming colonies under the supplied conditions contribute to the count.

Colony appearance does not establish species. An uninoculated control checks for visible background growth under the same conditions; no visible colonies do not prove universal absence of contamination.
questions.mistake: Counting the overgrown plate or forgetting the 0.100 cm³ volume and the dilution factor.
questions.tq: A 10⁻⁴ plate (0.100 cm³) has 120 colonies. What is the CFU per cm³ of the original suspension?

questions.title: Methylene blue staining: what a simple stain can and cannot show
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional methylene blue slide notes. The calibrated eyepiece scale is 2.5 µm per division at the objective used.
questions.question: Explain what a simple stain such as methylene blue shows, calculate the actual size of each cell type, identify the likely group of each, and state what cannot be concluded.
marks: Methylene blue is a simple (single dye) stain: it colours cells against a pale background so shape, arrangement and size can be seen.
Slide 1 rod length = 2.0 × 2.5 = 5.0 µm, a size typical of bacteria; the rods are likely bacteria.
Slide 2 diameter = 3.0 × 2.5 = 7.5 µm, 1.5 times the rod length, with buds: likely yeast, which are eukaryotic and reproduce by budding.
The stain does not give the species or the Gram reaction, so no species name or cell-wall type can be assigned from these slides.
Staining and fixation can distort appearance. A static fixed stained preparation cannot demonstrate active motility or growth, and it is not itself a viability or sterility test.

questions.practical_title: Cathode-ray properties in a demonstrated apparatus
questions.title: Cathode rays: properties and the charge-to-mass ratio
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results from a demonstration with a cathode-ray tube. For the speed measurement the electric and magnetic deflections cancel when E = 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 1.5 × 10⁻³ T. With the magnetic field alone, the beam moves on a circle of radius 0.0758 m. Assume mutually perpendicular electric/magnetic fields with the beam perpendicular to both; use the nonrelativistic model.
questions.question: Deduce three properties of cathode rays from the table, calculate the beam speed and the charge-to-mass ratio, and state what the ratio cannot give.
marks: The sharp shadow supports straight-line travel in a field-free region. Paddle-wheel motion is supporting evidence of energy/momentum transfer; by itself it is not a unique quantitative demonstration of electron mass.
Deflection towards the positive plate, reversing with polarity, shows the particles are negatively charged.
Balanced forces: eE = evB, so v = E ÷ B = 3.0 × 10⁴ ÷ 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
With the magnetic field alone, evB = mv²/r, so e/m = v ÷ (Br) = 2.0 × 10⁷ ÷ (1.5 × 10⁻³ × 0.0758) = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹.
The same behaviour for different gases and metals suggests a universal particle (the electron); e/m is only a ratio, so charge and mass separately need another measurement.
questions.mistake: Using the radius in centimetres in an SI equation.
questions.tq: With E = 4.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 1.5 × 10⁻³ T in the balanced condition, what is the beam speed?

questions.practical_title: Molecular and ionic shapes using models
questions.title: Molecular shapes: electron-pair counts to shape and angle
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies electron-pair counts for four species A to D, which are CH₄, NH₃, H₂O and BF₃ in some order. The counts refer to the central atom.
questions.question: Name the shape and approximate bond angle of each species, rank the four bond angles, and explain the ranking.
marks: A (4 bonding pairs, no lone pair; CH₄) is tetrahedral with an angle of about 109.5°.
B (3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair; NH₃) is trigonal pyramidal with an angle of about 107°.
C (2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs; H₂O) is bent (V-shaped) with an angle of about 104.5°.
D (3 bonding pairs, no lone pair; BF₃) is trigonal planar with an angle of 120°.
Order: D > A > B > C. Lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is greater than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, so each lone pair squeezes the bond angles together.
questions.mistake: Counting only bonding pairs when naming the shape, so that NH₃ is called planar.

questions.practical_title: Estimating magnesium relative atomic mass from gas data
questions.title: Relative atomic mass of magnesium from gas data
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional completed results: 0.0480 g of magnesium reacted completely with excess dilute acid and 49.6 cm³ of hydrogen was collected over water at 298 K. The atmospheric pressure was 101.3 kPa and the vapour pressure of water at 298 K is taken as 3.2 kPa. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume collected-gas pressure equals atmospheric pressure before the water-vapour subtraction (liquid levels equal or hydrostatic correction already applied).
questions.question: Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium from these data, and explain the effect on your answer of (i) ignoring the water vapour pressure and (ii) an oxide layer on the magnesium.
marks: Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂, so n(Mg) = n(H₂).
The gas is saturated with water vapour: p(H₂) = 101.3 − 3.2 = 98.1 kPa.
M(Mg) = 0.0480 g / n(Mg) = about24.44 g mol-1; the corresponding dimensionless relative atomic mass is Ar≈24.4 (using the g mol-1 numerical equivalence).
Ignoring vapour pressure overestimates the hydrogen and gives Ar = 23.7 (too low); an oxide layer means less magnesium metal reacts per measured gram, so the hydrogen is lower and Ar is too high.
questions.mistake: Using the total pressure for hydrogen, or using cm³ with the SI gas constant.
questions.tq: If 0.0486 g of magnesium gave 0.00200 mol of hydrogen, what Ar results?

questions.title: s-block metals: reactivity trend (theory only)
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional summary notes. No student handling is involved.
questions.question: State the trend in reactivity down group 1 and group 2, calculate the fall in first ionisation energy from Li to K, and explain the trend.
marks: Reactivity with water increases down group 1: Li < Na < K.
The first ionisation energy falls from 520 to 419 kJ mol⁻¹, a decrease of 101 kJ mol⁻¹ (19.4%).
Down the group, the atoms are larger and have more shielding, so the outer electron is held less strongly and is lost more easily.
Group 2 shows the same trend: Mg shows no visible reaction with cold water while Ca reacts steadily.
Reaction rate also depends on surface oxide, melting point and the heat released, so first ionisation energy is only one factor.
questions.mistake: Linking reactivity to atomic number alone without mentioning ionisation energy or shielding.
questions.tq: Rubidium has a first ionisation energy of 403 kJ mol⁻¹. Is it expected to be more or less reactive than potassium?
questions.ta: More reactive: its ionisation energy is lower and its atom is larger.

questions.title: Nitrogen in air: reading a control experiment
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results of burning magnesium. No student handling is involved.
questions.question: Explain how these results show that air contains nitrogen, write the two equations involved, and explain the role of the control.
marks: In air magnesium forms white magnesium oxide and a yellow-grey magnesium nitride.
Damp red litmus turning blue shows an alkaline gas (ammonia), so nitrogen from the air was combined in the ash.

The results show that nitrogen is present, not how much; litmus detects an alkaline gas, so a second test such as white fumes with hydrochloric acid supports ammonia.

Y is bromide: cream silver bromide, soluble only in concentrated ammonia.

questions.title: Ammonia and ammonium salts: observations and yield
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results: 0.535 g of a pure ammonium chloride sample was warmed with excess sodium hydroxide solution and all the ammonia was collected as a gas at a temperature where one mole of gas occupies 24.0 dm³. M(NH₄Cl) = 53.5 g mol⁻¹.

questions.practical_title: Solubility of s-block salts: trends and exceptions
questions.title: s-block salt solubility: Ksp and the opposite hydroxide trend
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies illustrative solubility product values at 298 K for the sulfates of group 2 metals, together with a qualitative note on the hydroxides. For these calculations use concentrations as activities, assume complete1:1 dissociation in pure water, neglect ion pairing, and exclude common ions.
questions.question: State the sulfate and hydroxide trends down group 2, calculate the molar solubility of BaSO₄ and CaSO₄ and their ratio, and give one reason the Ksp values of different salt types cannot be compared directly.
marks: Sulfate solubility decreases down group 2: CaSO₄ > SrSO₄ > BaSO₄, as the Ksp values fall.
For a 1:1 salt s = √Ksp, so s(BaSO₄) = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³.
s(CaSO₄) = √(4.9 × 10⁻⁵) = 7.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 6.7 × 10² times more soluble than BaSO₄.
The hydroxide trend is the opposite: solubility increases down group 2 (Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ is much more soluble).
The trends reflect the balance between lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpy as the cation grows; Ksp values can be compared directly only for salts with the same formula type.
questions.mistake: Comparing the Ksp of a 1:1 salt with that of a 1:2 salt as if it were solubility.
questions.tq: The Ksp of SrSO₄ is 3.4 × 10⁻⁷. What is its molar solubility?

questions.title: Thermal stability of group 2 carbonates
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies illustrative decomposition temperatures and a mass-loss record. M(CaCO₃) = 100.1 g mol⁻¹; M(CO₂) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹. No student handling is involved.

marks: Thermal stability of group 2 carbonates increases down the group (540 to 1300 °C).
Smaller cations with greater charge density polarise the carbonate ion more strongly, weakening the C–O bond; polarising power falls down the group.

questions.title: Alkenes and alkynes: bromine data and unsaturation
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results for three hydrocarbons, X (C₄H₆), Y (C₄H₈) and Z (C₄H₁₀), tested with bromine water in the dark. No student handling is involved. Assume all candidates are ordinary acyclic hydrocarbons and recorded uptake represents complete addition to their multiple bonds.
questions.question: Interpret the results for X, Y and Z, calculate the degree of unsaturation of each formula, and state a limitation of the bromine water test.
marks: Y adds one mole of Br₂ per mole: it has one C=C double bond (an alkene).
X adds two moles of Br₂ per mole: one C≡C triple bond or two C=C bonds (an alkyne or a diene) fits C₄H₆.
Z does not react in the dark: it is saturated (an alkane); substitution would need ultraviolet light.
Degree of unsaturation = (2C + 2 − H) ÷ 2 gives 2 for C₄H₆, 1 for C₄H₈ and 0 for C₄H₁₀, matching the bromine results.
Decolourisation is not specific to alkenes, because other unsaturated or reducing compounds can also react, so a second test is needed.
questions.mistake: Saying that Z reacts slowly with bromine water because it is unreactive, instead of saturated.
questions.tq: A hydrocarbon C₅H₈ absorbs 2 mol of H₂ per mole. What does this indicate?

questions.question: Classify alcohols 1, 2 and 3 as primary, secondary or tertiary with the product of oxidation, explain the colour change, and explain why alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass.
marks: Alcohol 1 is primary: it is oxidised to an aldehyde, which gives the silver mirror.
Alcohol 2 is secondary: it is oxidised to a ketone, which reacts with 2,4-DNPH but not with Tollens' reagent.
Alcohol 3 is tertiary: the carbon bearing the –OH has no hydrogen, so it resists oxidation.
The orange dichromate(VI) is reduced to green chromium(III) when an alcohol is oxidised.

questions.title: Phenol: weak acidity and ring activation
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results for aqueous phenol, C₆H₅OH, with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³ for the acid at 298 K.
questions.question: Explain what the first two tests show about the acidity of phenol, calculate the pH of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ phenol, explain the bromine result, and say why phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
marks: Phenol forms phenoxide with OH-. No CO2 effervescence from carbonate means it does not drive the full carbonate-to-carbonic-acid/CO2 process under this comparison. This does not exclude some carbonate-to-hydrogencarbonate proton transfer.
Bromine water is decolourised at once with a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, because the –OH group activates the ring.
The phenoxide charge is delocalised into the ring, stabilising the ion, which makes phenol more acidic than ethanol.

Violet colour with neutral FeCl3 supports phenolic chemistry but is not absolutely unique. The weak-acid calculation assumes[H+]≈sqrt(Ka c), negligible water autoionisation and small dissociation relative to c.

questions.title: Aldehydes and ketones: group tests and their overlaps
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional test records for three liquids A, B and C. No student handling is involved. Assume successful validated tests, no interfering compounds, and restrict candidates to simple aldehydes, ketones and monohydric alcohols. Interpret negatives only within that defined candidate set.
questions.question: Classify A, B and C using the tests, and explain why the iodoform result alone does not prove a carbonyl group.
marks: A positive 2,4-DNPH test for A and B shows that each contains a carbonyl group (C=O).
A is an aldehyde: it is oxidised by Tollens' reagent, giving the silver mirror.
B is a ketone: it does not reduce Tollens' reagent, and the yellow iodoform solid shows a CH₃–C(=O)– group (a methyl ketone).
C does not contain a carbonyl group (DNPH negative); its yellow iodoform solid arises from a CH₃CH(OH)– group such as in ethanol.
So the iodoform test alone does not prove a carbonyl group; these are group tests, and identity needs, for example, the melting point of a derivative.
questions.mistake: Concluding that a positive iodoform test means the compound is a ketone.
questions.tq: Which of A, B and C could be propanone?
questions.ta: B (carbonyl present, Tollens' negative, iodoform positive).

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional measured pH values at 298 K: 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid has pH 1.00 and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid has pH 2.88. Ethanoic acid also releases CO₂ from sodium carbonate solution.
questions.question: Calculate [H⁺], the percentage ionisation and Ka for ethanoic acid, compare [H⁺] with that of the hydrochloric acid, and explain what the carbonate result shows.
marks: Let c0=0.100mol dm-3 and x=[H+]=10^-2.88. Then Ka=x^2/(c0-x)≈1.76×10^-5mol dm-3 in the concentration approximation.
The hydrochloric acid [H⁺] is 0.100, about 76 times larger, so ethanoic acid is a weak acid that ionises only partly.

questions.title: Tests for aniline: basicity and diazonium chemistry
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional reference and test data. The pKa values are for the conjugate acids: anilinium 4.6 and ethylammonium 10.7.
questions.question: Explain why aniline is a weaker base than ethylamine and calculate the factor from the pKa values, explain the bromine result, and explain the effect of temperature on the diazonium test.
marks: In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept a proton.
The factor is 10^(10.7 − 4.6) = 10^6.1 = 1.3 × 10⁶ (the ethylammonium ion is that many times weaker as an acid, so ethylamine is the far stronger base).
Bromine water gives an immediate white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline because the –NH₂ group activates the ring.

Cold aqueous conditions help preserve the aromatic diazonium intermediate; warming accelerates decomposition with N2 evolution and can reduce the subsequent dye signal. This is not a universal stability boundary for every diazonium salt.
The orange-red azo dye shows coupling, but these are group tests; a single observation does not identify a compound.
questions.mistake: Saying that aniline is more basic because nitrogen has a lone pair.
questions.tq: Why must the diazotisation be kept at 0–5 °C?
questions.ta: The diazonium ion decomposes to nitrogen on warming.

questions.title: NO₂ / N₂O₄ equilibrium: temperature and Kc (theory)
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional notes for 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH = −57 kJ mol⁻¹. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. Kc = 170 dm³ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. A sealed tube is brown at 298 K, much paler in ice-water and darker brown in hot water.
questions.question: Explain the colour changes, write the expression for Kc, calculate [N₂O₄] when [NO₂] = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³ at 298 K, state which change alters Kc, and state a limitation of using colour.
marks: The forward reaction is exothermic, so cooling shifts the equilibrium right (more colourless N₂O₄, paler) and heating shifts it left (more brown NO₂, darker).
Only a change of temperature changes Kc; here Kc decreases as temperature rises. A catalyst or a change of concentration does not alter Kc.
Colour depends on path length and amounts as well as on temperature, and heating a sealed tube also raises its pressure, so colour is qualitative evidence only.
questions.mistake: Saying that a catalyst shifts the equilibrium position or changes Kc.
questions.tq: At the same temperature, what is [N₂O₄] when [NO₂] = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³?

questions.title: Na₂CO₃ with HCl: two indicators, two end points
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional completed titration results: 25.00 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sodium carbonate was titrated with hydrochloric acid. The phenolphthalein end point (pink to colourless) was at 10.25 cm³ and the methyl orange end point, reached by continuing the titration, was at a total of 20.50 cm³.
questions.question: Write the equations for the two stages, calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid, check the two end points for consistency, and explain one limitation of the methyl orange end point.
marks: Stage 1: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻ (phenolphthalein). Stage 2: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O (methyl orange). Overall: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O.
n(HCl) at the total end point = 2 × 1.250 × 10⁻³ = 2.500 × 10⁻³ mol, so c(HCl) = 2.500 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.02050 = 0.122 mol dm⁻³.
The first end point (10.25 cm³) is exactly half of the total (20.50 cm³), as 1:1 then 1:1 stoichiometry predicts.
Dissolved CO₂ makes the methyl orange end point gradual and the colour change is judged by eye, so the volume has a reading uncertainty; indicators are chosen by the pH at each equivalence point.
questions.mistake: Using a 1:1 mole ratio for the overall reaction.
questions.tq: If the total methyl orange end point had been 22.00 cm³, what would c(HCl) be?

questions.title: Standard electrodes: converting between reference electrodes
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional measurements of two half-cells made against a saturated calomel reference electrode (SCE), whose potential is +0.241 V relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). All ion concentrations are 1.00 mol dm⁻³ at 298 K.

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional data for an immiscible oil–water mixture that boils at 98.0 °C under 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of water at 98.0 °C is 94.3 kPa. The oil component has M = 136 g mol⁻¹ and water M = 18.0 g mol⁻¹. Assume ideal vapours.

questions.title: Spherometer: radius of curvature and the dominant uncertainty
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional readings. The spherometer screw has a pitch of 1.0 mm and the circular scale has 100 divisions. The mean distance between the legs is l = 30.0 mm and the measured height (sagitta) is h = 0.400 mm, read to ±0.01 mm. Use R = l² ÷ (6h) + h ÷ 2.
questions.question: Find the least count, calculate the radius of curvature, and estimate the uncertainty in R assuming the error in h dominates.
marks: Least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions = 1.0 mm ÷ 100 = 0.01 mm.
Because h is small, ±0.01 mm in 0.400 mm is 2.5%, and R is roughly proportional to 1/h, so R is uncertain by about 2.5% (±9.4 mm).
Report R = (375 ± 9) mm; a small sagitta is the weak point, so l and h should be measured carefully and h repeated.
questions.mistake: Using the leg distance as a diameter or forgetting the h ÷ 2 term.

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results for light inside a glass prism meeting a glass–air surface: at an angle of incidence of 41.0° a faint refracted ray still emerges; at 42.5° the light is totally internally reflected.
questions.question: Estimate the critical angle, calculate the refractive index and its range, and state the conditions for total internal reflection.
marks: The critical angle lies between 41.0° and 42.5°; the best estimate is the midpoint, C = 41.75° (about 41.8°).
The bracketing angles give n from 1 ÷ sin 42.5° = 1.48 to 1 ÷ sin 41.0° = 1.52, so n = 1.50 ± 0.02.
Total internal reflection needs light travelling from the denser to the less dense medium with an angle of incidence greater than C.
C depends on wavelength (dispersion), so white light gives a slightly blurred boundary; a narrower bracket would reduce the uncertainty.

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional readings for a uniform quill tube with air trapped by a 10.0 cm mercury thread. questions.title: Pressure against temperature at constant volume
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional readings for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume.
questions.question: Calculate the gradient, find the temperature at which the pressure would extrapolate to zero, test whether p/T is constant using kelvin, and state two limitations.
marks: Gradient = (136.6 − 100.0) ÷ 100 = 0.366 kPa K⁻¹ (a step of 1 °C equals 1 K).
This intercept is the absolute zero of the kelvin scale: T / K = θ / °C + 273.15.
p/T is constant: 100.0 ÷ 273.15 = 0.3661 and 136.6 ÷ 373.15 = 0.3661 kPa K⁻¹, so p ∝ T in kelvin.
The extrapolation is far outside the data, real gases liquefy before 0 K, and expansion of the vessel means the volume is not perfectly constant.

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results: a 0.250 kg metal block at 100.0 °C is transferred into 0.200 kg of water at 20.0 °C in a calorimeter of heat capacity 100 J K⁻¹. The final steady temperature is 27.4 °C. Take c(water) = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.question: Calculate the heat gained by the water and calorimeter, the specific heat capacity of the metal, the value obtained if the calorimeter is ignored, and the effect of heat loss during transfer.

questions.title: Specific heat capacity of a liquid by the method of cooling
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results for the same calorimeter (heat capacity 40 J K⁻¹), filled in turn with equal volumes of water and of a liquid, and cooled from 60 °C to 50 °C under the same conditions. questions.title: Specific latent heat of fusion of ice by mixtures
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results: 0.050 kg of surface-dried water ice at 0 °C is added to 0.200 kg of water at 40.0 °C in a calorimeter of heat capacity 100 J K⁻¹. The final temperature is 18.1 °C. Take c(water) = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
questions.question: Write the energy balance, calculate the specific latent heat of fusion, and explain the effect of using wet ice.
marks: Heat lost by water and calorimeter = heat to melt the ice + heat to warm the melted ice from 0 °C to the final temperature.
Heat to warm the melt water = 0.050 × 4180 × 18.1 = 3783 J.
Wet ice includes water that needs no melting, so the true ice mass is smaller than recorded and L is underestimated; the ice should be dried first.

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results: dry steam at 100 °C is passed into 0.200 kg of water at 20.0 °C in a calorimeter of heat capacity 100 J K⁻¹ until the temperature is 40.0 °C. The mass gain is 0.0075 kg (7.5 g). Take c(water) = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.title: Thermal conductivity by Searle's method
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional steady-state readings for a lagged copper bar of diameter 2.00 cm. Thermometers 0.100 m apart along the bar differ by 10.0 K. Cooling water flows at 0.145 kg per 100 s and rises by 2.00 K. Take c(water) = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.practical_title: Internal resistance of a cell: potentiometer
questions.title: Internal resistance of a cell with a potentiometer
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional balance lengths with a steady driver current: with the cell on open circuit the balance length is l₁ = 70.0 cm; with a 10.0 Ω resistor across the cell it is l₂ = 62.0 cm. Each length is read to ±0.1 cm.
questions.question: Derive the expression for r, calculate it with its uncertainty, and state two conditions for the method.
marks: E ∝ l₁ (no current drawn at balance) and the terminal p.d. V ∝ l₂.
E = I(R + r) and V = IR, so l₁ ÷ l₂ = (R + r) ÷ R, giving r = R(l₁ − l₂) ÷ l₂.
The difference 8.0 cm carries ±0.2 cm (2.5%) and l₂ ±0.1 cm (0.2%), so r = 1.29 ± 0.03 Ω.
Conditions: the driver current (potential gradient) must not change between readings, and the resistor is connected only while balancing so the cell does not run down.

questions.title: Forward-biased diode: non-ohmic I–V data
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional forward-bias readings for a silicon diode.
questions.question: Describe the I–V relationship, state the approximate turn-on voltage, calculate the dynamic resistance between 0.70 V and 0.75 V and the static resistance at 0.75 V, and state a limitation.
marks: The current rises very steeply rather than in proportion to V, so the diode is non-ohmic.
Conduction becomes significant at about 0.6–0.7 V, typical of silicon.
Dynamic resistance = ΔV ÷ ΔI = 0.05 ÷ (0.030 − 0.012) = 2.8 Ω (it was 0.05 ÷ 0.008 = 6.25 Ω between 0.65 V and 0.70 V).
Static resistance at 0.75 V = V ÷ I = 0.75 ÷ 0.030 = 25.0 Ω; static and dynamic resistance differ for a non-linear device.
Heating at higher current changes the characteristic, and a series resistor is needed to limit the current.

questions.title: Transistor transfer characteristic: current gain
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional common-emitter readings at a fixed collector–emitter voltage.
questions.question: Calculate the a.c. current gain over the whole range, the d.c. gain at I_B = 30 µA, comment on linearity, and state a limitation.
marks: Over the range: (5.8 − 1.5) mA ÷ (40 − 10) µA = 4.3 mA ÷ 30 µA = 143.
d.c. gain at 30 µA: h_FE = I_C ÷ I_B = 4.4 mA ÷ 30 µA = 147.
The local gain is 150 from 10 to 20 µA and 140 above, so the transfer characteristic is nearly, but not exactly, linear.

Current gain can change with collector current and temperature. Because VCE is held fixed here, increasing current alone does not establish saturation; saturation may occur in a circuit if it can no longer maintain the intended active-region VCE.

questions.title: Viscosity of water by capillary flow (Poiseuille)
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional steady-flow results: capillary radius 0.250 mm, length 0.200 m, constant pressure head 0.300 m of water, and 1.00 cm³ collected in 44.3 s. Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.81 m s⁻². Interpret the viscosity calculation conditionally on the steady laminar Poiseuille model.
questions.question: Calculate pressure difference and viscosity under the Poiseuille model, explain the radius sensitivity and state why one head/flow observation cannot independently establish the laminar regime.
marks: Poiseuille: V/t = πr⁴ΔP ÷ (8ηL), so η = πr⁴ΔP t ÷ (8VL).
Because eta depends on r^4, a 2% radius error contributes approximately 8% uncertainty (8.24% for a 2% overestimate exactly). It dominates only if other relative contributions are smaller.

One pressure-head/flow pair cannot independently establish laminar Poiseuille flow. The handbook recommends the straight-line portion of a volume-flow-rate versus head graph; curvature at larger heads signals possible breakdown of that regime.
questions.mistake: Using the diameter instead of the radius, which changes η by a factor of 16.
questions.tq: If the radius were measured 2% too large, how would the calculated η change?

Reynolds-number thresholds are absent from this handbook method; use its Q-versus-head evidence criterion. Radius dominance also requires comparison with other uncertainties.

questions.practical_title: Surface tension from a microscope slide
questions.title: Surface tension using a microscope slide
questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional results: a clean slide 25.0 mm wide and 1.0 mm thick touches a water surface; just before it pulls free, the extra pull (after allowing for weight and upthrust) corresponds to a mass of 0.382 g. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻² and a contact angle of zero.
questions.question: Calculate the length of the contact line, the surface-tension force and the surface tension, find the error from ignoring the slide thickness, and state two assumptions.
marks: The contact line runs round the slide: 2(l + t) = 2(0.0250 + 0.0010) = 0.0520 m.
Ignoring the thickness, γ = F ÷ 2l = 0.0749 N m⁻¹, about 4.0% too high.
Assumptions: contact angle is zero and the recorded force is the net additional surface pull. Contamination can alter wetting/contact angle; detergent in the water can lower its surface tension.
questions.mistake: Using only one face of the slide (length l) as the contact line.

questions.scenario: A teacher supplies fictional readings: air bubbles form slowly at the tip of a capillary of radius 0.500 mm held 1.00 cm below a water surface. Subtract the depth: h − d = 3.94 − 1.00 = 2.94 cm of water.
